props.title: Words and Music
props.initialSlug: Rodgers & Hart's musical legacy comes alive on screen

sections.content: **Words and Music** (1948) represents MGM's glossy but fictionalized take on the legendary songwriting partnership of Richard Rodgers and Lorenz Hart. The film showcases the incredible musical legacy of the duo through lavish production numbers, though it notably sanitizes Hart's troubled personal life and sexuality. Mickey Rooney's energetic portrayal of Hart and Tom Drake's measured Rodgers anchor a film that prioritizes spectacular musical sequences over biographical accuracy. The film follows a pattern established by earlier composer biopics like Night and Day (1946) about Cole Porter, where Hollywood's tendency to mythologize its subjects resulted in heightened entertainment value at the expense of historical truth.

sections.content: The film's greatest strength lies in its musical numbers, featuring some of the era's biggest stars performing Rodgers & Hart classics. Judy Garland delivers a show-stopping "Johnny One Note," while Gene Kelly and Vera-Ellen dazzle in "Slaughter on Tenth Avenue." These sequences exemplify the peak of MGM's musical unit under producer Arthur Freed, following the template of successful anthology films like **Ziegfeld Follies** (1946) where the emphasis was on spectacular individual performances rather than narrative cohesion.

The biographical musical trend continued through the 1940s and 50s with films like Three Little Words (1950) about songwriters Bert Kalmar and Harry Ruby, and **I'll See You in My Dreams** (1951) about Gus Kahn. These films established a formula of presenting sanitized versions of composers' lives while using their music as a framework for elaborate production numbers. **Words and Music** particularly influenced later composer biopics in its approach to balancing biographical elements with pure entertainment. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Musical Biopics

sections.content: While **Words and Music** took significant liberties with its subject matter, it set important precedents for how Hollywood would approach musical biographies. Later films like **De-Lovely** (2004) about Cole Porter and **Beyond the Sea** (2004) about Bobby Darin would attempt more honest portrayals of their subjects' personal lives while maintaining the musical showcase format. The contrast between these later works and **Words and Music** highlights how biographical films have evolved to embrace more complex narratives while still celebrating the musical legacy of their subjects.
